header_title: One Percent Too Many Electrons
tagline: How a tiny charge imbalance could lift the Earth
question_text: What if two people each carried 1% more electrons than protons?
audio_script: Imagine you and a friend, an arm's length apart. Now suppose that magically, each of you had just one percent more electrons than protons. What happens? The electric repulsion would be staggering. Enough to lift the Empire State Building? No. Everest? Still no. Enough to lift the Earth? Closer. The electric force is ten to the thirty-sixth times stronger than gravity. Yet we feel nothing, because every proton pull cancels every electron push in the fine balance of matter. That is why the chair is stiff and why you are not electrocuted by sitting on it. And it is also why matter resists being squeezed - tiny imbalances between neighbouring atoms are holding everything in place.

header_title: The Invisible Glue of Matter
tagline: Why atoms stay locked in a crystal
question_text: How does a tiny imbalance of charge make solids stiff?
audio_script: A crystal of salt looks still. But inside, every positive sodium ion is pulling on every chloride ion and pushing on every other sodium. Why doesn't it fly apart? The secret is balance. Each atom feels push and pull from all sides, and they cancel almost exactly. In the small gaps between atoms, though, the cancellation is not perfect. That tiny leftover - a fraction of a fraction - is what glues the crystal together. The very same imperfect balance makes your table resist your hand, your bone resist your weight, your building resist the wind. All the stiffness in the world is just leftover electrical force.

header_title: The Quantum Wobble That Keeps You Solid
tagline: Why electrons don't crash into the nucleus
question_text: If opposites attract
option_a: why don't electrons spiral into protons?
audio_script: [{"type":"orbit","id":"electron_orbit","center":[0,0,0],"width":5,"height":3,"period":6,"body_radius":0.18,"body_color":"#4CC9F0","orbit_color":"#8A8F9C"},{"type":"charge","id":"nucleus","pos":[0,0,0],"radius":0.28,"color":"#FF4B4B","label":"+"}]
orientation: Common sense says electrons should fall into protons. They attract, they are close, they have nothing to stop them. But they don't. Why? Quantum mechanics. If an electron is squeezed into a tiny region, the uncertainty principle gives it a huge momentum - a wild, jittery energy that fights the attraction. Balance the two and you get a stable atom. The electron sits at just the distance where the electric pull equals the quantum push. Take away the quantum wobble and matter would collapse in a flash. The universe is held up by uncertainty.

header_title: The Complete Force Law
tagline: F = q(E + v×B) - one equation for all of electromagnetism
question_text: What is the full force on a moving charge?
audio_script: Every force in electromagnetism - every motor, every speaker, every aurora - comes from one equation. The force on a charge is q times the electric field plus q times v cross B. That's it. Electric field pushes along, magnetic field pushes sideways, always perpendicular to motion. Make a magnetic field bigger, the charge bends harder. Reverse its sign, the push flips. Even light is just this equation, run for a wave. Maxwell's equations tell the fields where to be. Lorentz tells the charges where to go. Between them, all of radio, radar, X-rays, and glowing plasma.

header_title: Fields Add Like Arrows
tagline: The simplest and deepest principle in electromagnetism
question_text: How do you handle two charges at once?
audio_script: Two charges push on you at once. What do you do? You cheat - you solve them one at a time and add the answers. Add the two arrows, tail to tail, tip to tip. That's superposition. It sounds trivial. It isn't. Every electric and magnetic field you have ever seen is built this way: one charge at a time, then sum. Maxwell's equations are linear - the whole edifice of radio and light stands on this quiet assumption. But look at field lines for two charges and you'll see the dark side. Lines crossing? Impossible. The picture breaks, the mathematics does not. Superposition is easy in the algebra, awkward in the art.

header_title: How Much Field Flows Through?
tagline: The idea behind Gauss's law
question_text: What does it mean to count field lines through a surface?
audio_script: Imagine the electric field as water flowing outward from a charge. Now draw a closed surface around the charge. How much water crosses per second? That is the flux. If the charge is inside, the flux is the same no matter what surface you draw - tiny sphere, lumpy bag, big cube. If the charge is outside, whatever goes in also comes out; net flux is zero. This single rule, Gauss's law, is Coulomb's inverse square restated. It is also the gateway to almost every shortcut in electrostatics.

header_title: Detecting the Swirl
tagline: The idea behind Ampere's law
question_text: How do you measure how much a field circles a loop?
audio_script: Freeze a fluid. Now cut a thin tube through it, following some closed loop. Inside that tube the liquid keeps circulating - the momentum is trapped. The speed of circulation times the circumference is what we call circulation. For a magnetic field around a wire, the same idea applies. Walk a closed curve, dot each B with the little step forward, sum them up. That number tells you how much current is threading through your loop. That is Ampere's law. It is the magnetic twin of Gauss's law.

header_title: The Gap in Ampere's Law
tagline: How a changing electric field creates magnetism
question_text: What fixes the fact that Ampere's law fails in a charging capacitor?
audio_script: Ampère's law works beautifully for a steady current. Then Maxwell noticed a flaw. Charge a capacitor: current flows in the wires, stops at the gap. Draw a surface across the wire - current passes through. Draw it through the gap - no current. Same loop, two answers. Something must be missing. Maxwell proposed: a changing electric field is itself a current. Add that displacement current and the loop works everywhere. The universe works. Without this fix, no light could travel through empty space.

header_title: Magnetism = Moving Electricity
tagline: Why magnetic forces are tiny relativistic leftovers
question_text: Why does moving a magnet next to a wire generate a current?
audio_script: Here is a secret. Magnetism is not a separate force. It is electricity, viewed from another frame. Two protons travelling side by side repel electrically. Now run alongside them. They're at rest - pure electric. In your frame there's a magnetic field. In theirs there isn't. So is magnetism real? Yes, as a relativistic correction. In a wire, electrons drift at a tenth of a millimetre per second. v squared over c squared is ten to the minus twenty-five. But the electric force has cancelled to better than that. Only the tiny magnetic correction remains - and it moves motors, makes compass needles spin, paints the aurora.

header_title: The Picture Is Not the Thing
tagline: Why physicists gave up on visualising fields
question_text: What's wrong with drawing field lines?
audio_script: For a hundred years, physicists drew field lines. Beautiful pictures - arrows from positive to negative, denser where the field is strong. Then relativity arrived. Ride along with a magnet at light speed - its B field disappears. Lines can't disappear. They're not real. Neither are they useless. The field's the thing - a mathematical object at every point in space, whether or not anyone draws it. Field lines are shadows on the wall. Useful for the intuition, dangerous for the soul.

tagline: Order-of-magnitude reasoning with Coulomb's law
question_text: Two 70 kg people stand 1 m apart. If each had 1% more electrons than protons
option_a: roughly how large is the repulsive force between them?

orientation: Start with the number of protons. A 70 kg body is about seventy kilograms of mostly water - roughly seven times ten to the twenty-eight nucleons. One percent of that is a charge imbalance of seven times ten to the twenty-six elementary charges. Multiply by 1.6 times ten to the minus nineteen coulombs: about ten to the seventh coulombs on each body. Now Coulomb: F equals k q squared over r squared. k is nine times ten to the ninth. q squared is ten to the fourteenth. r squared is one. So F comes out around ten to the twenty-fifth newtons. That's the weight of the entire Earth. Two people, an arm's length apart. That's the electric force you never feel.

header_title: Electric vs Gravitational Force Between Protons
tagline: The famous 10^36 ratio
question_text: Two protons separated by 10^-15 m. How many times stronger is the electric repulsion than gravitational attraction?
audio_script: Both forces go as one over r squared. That's the trick - the distance cancels. So the ratio is a pure number: electric strength divided by gravitational strength. Electric: k e squared. That's nine times ten to the ninth, times 1.6 times ten to the minus nineteen, squared. Roughly 2.3 times ten to the minus twenty-eight. Gravitational: G m squared. Six point seven times ten to the minus eleven, times 1.67 times ten to the minus twenty-seven, squared. That's 1.9 times ten to the minus sixty-four. Divide one by the other: ten to the thirty-six. A million billion billion. The reason you don't fly apart and don't collapse is that these are so precisely balanced in every atom.

question_text: A proton moves at 3×10^6 m/s along +x. E = 2×10^5 V/m along +y
option_a: B = 0.5 T along +z. What is the net force vector?

Add them: the electric push is tiny, the magnetic push dominates. Net is about 2.1 times ten to the minus thirteen newtons pointing in minus y.

header_title: Two Equal Positive Charges
tagline: Where does the field vanish?
question_text: Two +q charges sit at x = -a and x = +a. What is the electric field at (i) x = 0 and (ii) x = 3a?
option_b: 2kq/a^2 at x = 0; kq/4a^2 along -x at x = 3a
option_d: kq/a^2 at x = 0; kq/2a^2 along +x at x = 3a
audio_script: By symmetry at the midpoint, each charge pushes with equal strength in opposite directions. Net is exactly zero. Now go to x equals three a. That is two a from the right charge, four a from the left. Field from the right: k q over four a squared, pointing away from it - toward plus x. Field from the left: k q over sixteen a squared, pointing away - toward minus x. Subtract: three k q over sixteen a squared, plus x direction. Notice the field is not just one over distance squared from a single point - it is a sum. Superposition is doing the work.

header_title: Flux Through a Surface That Misses the Charge
tagline: Why 'inside' matters in Gauss's law
question_text: A +q charge sits just outside a closed spherical surface. What is the net electric flux through the surface?
audio_script: Gauss's law has a deceptively simple statement: flux through any closed surface equals the enclosed charge over epsilon zero. A charge outside the surface? Zero. Why? Every field line that enters must exit. They are not created or destroyed in empty space. Pick a field line skimming in, count it. Follow it through - it comes out. Count again. One plus, one minus. Zero. Now put the charge inside. Every line that starts on it must end somewhere outside - count of outbound lines equals charge over epsilon zero. That is why Gauss's law is so powerful: the surface shape doesn't matter, only what is inside.

header_title: Circulation of B Around a Wire
tagline: Ampere's law in one calculation
question_text: A long straight wire carries 2 A. A circular loop of radius 0.5 m circles the wire. What is the line integral of B around the loop?
audio_script: Ampere's law does not ask you to compute B. It just asks for the integral. In SI units, epsilon zero c squared is exactly four pi times ten to the minus seven. Multiply by the enclosed current of two amperes. That is eight pi times ten to the minus seven, roughly 2.5 times ten to the minus six tesla metres. The radius of the loop does not appear. Any loop surrounding the wire gives this same integral - one metre, one kilometre, tangled, circular, anything. Only when the wire is outside does the answer drop to zero. Ampere's law is a bookkeeping shortcut: how much current threads your loop?

header_title: Which Way Does the Magnetic Force Point?
tagline: A right-hand-rule test
question_text: An electron moves east at speed v through a magnetic field pointing north. Which direction does the magnetic force act on it?
audio_script: Right-hand rule first. Index finger east, middle finger north. Thumb points up. That would be the force on a positive charge. But our particle is an electron - negative. Flip the direction. Down. This is the kind of trap exams love. The rule is for a positive charge; for an electron the actual force is opposite. So the electron gets pushed downward, into the page if you want to be precise about the geometry. This is why electrons in a cathode ray tube bend one way while protons bend the other for the same v and B. The arrow from v cross B is what a positive charge would feel.

header_title: Two Parallel Wires
tagline: Same Current Direction
question_text: How strong is the attraction?
option_d: 0.1 m apart. What is the force per unit length?
audio_script: 8x10^-6 N/m attractive
column17: First, direction. Same-direction currents attract. Opposite-direction currents repel. That's the magnetic equivalent of a handshake. Now the magnitude: mu zero times I one I two over two pi d. mu zero is four pi times ten to the minus seven. I one times I two is eight. Two pi d is two pi times 0.1, which is 0.2 pi. Cancel pi, get four times ten to the minus seven, times eight, over 0.2. That is thirty-two times ten to the minus seven over 0.2, which is 1.6 times ten to the minus five newtons per metre. Small, but real. This is how current balances work - the magnetic attraction between coils calibrates the ampere.

header_title: The Rate of Change of E Between Capacitor Plates
tagline: Maxwell's missing term - quantified
question_text: A parallel-plate capacitor of area 0.01 m^2 is charged at 5 A. What is dE/dt between the plates?
audio_script: Maxwell's displacement current equals epsilon zero times dE/dt times area. That must equal the actual current in the wire - five amperes. So dE/dt equals I over epsilon zero times area. Five over eight point eight five times ten to the minus twelve, times one hundredth. That is five over eight point eight five times ten to the minus fourteen. Roughly five point six five times ten to the thirteen volts per metre per second. Staggering number. But notice: no matter how large, it is required for the loop integral of B to match. The changing E between the plates acts like a real current. That is why electromagnetic waves can travel in vacuum - E changes create B, B changes create E, no charges needed.

tagline: The v squared over c squared in the fine print
question_text: In a copper wire with electron drift speed 0.1 mm/s
option_a: what is v^2/c^2 - the tiny ratio hiding in every magnetic force?

orientation: Drift velocity is a tenth of a millimetre per second, so ten to the minus four metres per second. Square that: ten to the minus eight. c squared is nine times ten to the sixteen. Divide: about ten to the minus twenty-five. Absurdly small. So why does magnetism matter at all? Because the electric field between moving electrons in two parallel wires is not small - it is enormous - but it also almost perfectly cancels the proton's opposite field. The cancellation is good to far better than ten to the minus twenty-five. Only the tiny leftover remains. That leftover is magnetism. What we call magnetic force is the relativistic tail of an almost perfectly balanced electric force.
